Marie Antoinette. Born in 1755 in Austria, this queen became the symbol of everything revolutionaries hated about royal excess and corruption. She was married to Louis XVI in 1770 as part of a diplomatic alliance between France and Austria, but she struggled with the rigid etiquette and isolation of court life. As the fiscal crisis deepened, she became increasingly unpopular. People blamed her for encouraging the king to resist reform and accused her of extravagance in dress and entertainment. The Flight to Varennes in 1791 was a turning point. When she and Louis XVI attempted to escape together, the failed attempt destroyed her image as a French queen and sealed the revolution's move toward radicalism. Revolutionaries alleged that she had encouraged royalist conspiracies and secret negotiations with foreign powers, fueling charges that she was a traitor selling France to Austria. During imprisonment, she was separated from her family. Her young son, the dauphin Louis-Charles, was taken from her and indoctrinated by revolutionaries. In October 1793, she was tried for high treason. Prosecutors also leveled charges of incest with her son, designed to dehumanize her in public eyes. She was executed by guillotine on October 16, 1793, less than nine months after her husband's death. She reportedly maintained composure and dignity on her way to the scaffold.
